identity.spiritualSignificanceShort: Jwalamukhi is one of the 51 Shakti Peethas of the subcontinent, at the site where, by tradition, the tongue of the goddess Sati fell. It holds no idol: worship centres on natural gas flames that burn continuously through fissures in the rock inside the sanctum, understood as nine forms of the goddess (the Navjyoti). The site is also associated with the legend of the devotee Dhyanu Bhagat and with a Mughal-era tradition that the emperor Akbar tried and failed to extinguish the flame.

narrative.summaryIntro:
Jwalamukhi Temple stands at about 600 m in the Kangra valley of Himachal Pradesh, in the Shivalik range. It is dedicated to the goddess in her form as Jwalamukhi ('flaming mouth') and is counted among the 51 Shakti Peethas. The sanctum holds no image: worship is offered to natural flames that burn continuously through fissures in the rock, fed by underground gas, and traditionally understood as nine forms of the goddess.

The earliest surviving textual reference to the site by name is in the 14th-century Tarikh-i-Firuz-Shahi of Shams-i Siraj, which records a visit by the Delhi Sultanate ruler Firuz Shah Tughlaq. The temple was visited by Mughal emperor Jahangir after the 1620 conquest of Kangra fort, and in 1809 the Sikh ruler Maharaja Ranjit Singh and Kangra's Raja Sansar Chand concluded a treaty at the temple. The temple's present golden dome and silver door are traditionally attributed to donations from Ranjit Singh and his son Kharak Singh. The temple is administered today by the Kangra district administration's Commissioner (Temple)-cum-Deputy Commissioner office together with a temple trust.
narrative.sthalaPuranam: Tradition holds that when the god Vishnu cut apart the body of the goddess Sati with his discus, her tongue fell at this site, making it one of the 51 Shakti Peethas. A widely told legend describes the Mughal emperor Akbar attempting to test or extinguish the temple's eternal flame — by building a water channel, covering it with iron vessels, and finally offering a gold umbrella — all of which the tradition says failed, with the umbrella said to have been transformed into an unidentifiable metal, still preserved at the temple. A related legend concerns the devotee Dhyanu Bhagat, said to have offered his own head to the goddess in Akbar's court and to have been restored to life; devotees are said to have since offered coconuts in place of the ancestral practice. These are traditional/devotional accounts and are not presented here as verified history.
narrative.documentedHistory: Jwalamukhi's earliest datable textual mention is in Shams-i Siraj's 14th-century Tarikh-i-Firuz-Shahi, describing a visit by Firuz Shah Tughlaq. Mughal emperor Jahangir is recorded to have visited the temple after Kangra fort's capture in 1620. Sixteenth- and seventeenth-century writers including Abul Fazl, Thomas Coryat and Jean de Thévenot also described the site's natural flames. In 1809, following the expulsion of Gorkha forces from Kangra, a treaty was concluded between Maharaja Ranjit Singh and Raja Sansar Chand of Kangra at the temple; Ranjit Singh's son Kharak Singh is credited with donating the temple's silver-plated doors. An idol form of the goddess was installed at the temple in 1965 by Raja Baldev Singh of the Guler dynasty, alongside the aniconic flame worship that remains central to the site. Hereditary worship rights belong to priests of the Bhojak community.

visitingInfo.nearestAirport: Gaggal Airport (Kangra), approximately 50 km via Dharamshala
visitingInfo.accessibilityNotes: The temple is about 50 km from the district headquarters, Dharamshala; approximately 200 km from Chandigarh, 118 km from Jalandhar, 105 km from Pathankot and 180 km from Shimla by road.
visitingInfo.officialContactNote: Contact the Office of the Commissioner (Temple)-cum-Deputy Commissioner, Kangra at Dharamshala (phone 01892-222705, email kangratemple@gmail.com) to confirm current darshan timings, festival dates and any entry rules before travelling.

openingHours.notes: Unlike the seasonal Himalayan Char Dham shrines, Jwalamukhi is open to devotees throughout the year. The official Kangra district temple portal does not publish specific daily opening and closing clock times, so none are recorded here.
